title: Apple News Becomes “Even More Politically Lopsided” Under New CEO John Ternus, Study Shows
body:
Apple’s news‑aggregation platform has come under fire this month after a conservative watchdog group reported that the service’s editorial mix heavily favored left‑leaning outlets during the first full month of John Ternus’s tenure as senior vice president of worldwide hardware engineering, a role that also oversees Apple News. The Media Research Center (MRC) said that, in September, 67 percent of the stories Apple News promoted originated from publications identified as liberal, a shift the group described as “decidedly leftist” compared with previous reporting periods.

The MRC’s analysis draws on a sample of 2,500 articles that appeared in the “Top Stories” carousel and the “For You” personalized feed for U.S. users. According to the study, outlets such as The New York Times, The Washington Post, CNN and MSNBC accounted for the majority of the highlighted content, while conservative sources like Fox News, The Wall Street Journal’s editorial page and Breitbart were markedly under‑represented. The organization argues that this imbalance reflects a broader trend of tech platforms curating news in a way that aligns with liberal perspectives, potentially influencing public discourse.

Apple, which has long positioned its news service as a neutral conduit for a wide range of publishers, declined to comment on the specific findings but reiterated its commitment to “providing diverse, high‑quality journalism to our users.” In a brief statement, the company noted that its algorithms are designed to surface stories that are “relevant and engaging” based on individual reading habits, and that editorial teams regularly review content for compliance with Apple’s policies on misinformation and hate speech. The firm has not disclosed any changes to its curation methodology since Ternus assumed his expanded responsibilities in August.

Industry observers caution that the MRC’s methodology and partisan framing may limit the study’s broader applicability. Media analyst Priya Desai of the Brookings Institution highlighted that algorithmic recommendation systems are inherently complex, balancing factors such as user engagement, source credibility, and timeliness. “A single month’s snapshot can be skewed by news cycles—think of the heightened coverage of climate policy, voting rights and international conflicts, which happen to be dominated by liberal outlets,” she said. Desai added that Apple’s lack of transparency around its recommendation engine makes it difficult for external parties to verify claims of bias, a challenge common to most digital news aggregators.

The controversy arrives at a moment when scrutiny of tech‑mediated news distribution is intensifying. Recent congressional hearings and antitrust investigations have focused on how platforms prioritize content, with lawmakers from both parties expressing concern that algorithmic curation can amplify certain viewpoints while marginalizing others. In response, several major tech firms have pledged to increase transparency, publish bias‑assessment reports and, in some cases, allow users to customize their news sources more directly. Apple’s upcoming iOS 18 update, slated for release later this year, is rumored to include new settings that let users “weight” the political spectrum of their news feed, though Apple has not confirmed the feature.

Looking ahead, the debate over Apple News’ editorial balance is likely to persist as the company refines its content strategy under Ternus’s leadership. If the platform’s algorithm continues to favor stories from liberal publications, it could prompt further criticism from conservative groups and potentially spur regulatory inquiries. Conversely, Apple may respond by enhancing its disclosure practices or adjusting its recommendation logic to demonstrate a more equitable distribution of viewpoints. As the news ecosystem evolves, the pressure on tech companies to prove impartiality—and to provide users with clearer insight into how stories are selected—will remain a central theme in the ongoing conversation about media, technology and democracy.
